 "sections":{
  "trigger":{"covered":true,"evidence":[
    {"id":"E1","excerpt":"Their ecommerce director, Lucy, came inbound.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E2","excerpt":"She said about one in twelve online orders was failing at the payment step, and it was worse on the big baskets.","label":"fact"},

   "insight":"The deal began with a measurable revenue leak: one in twelve online orders failing, worse on high-value items, and the figure came from the customer's own dashboard. We had a number we could have priced from the first call. A second pain, the incumbent's lack of explanation, went unused even though Lucy raised it herself.","messaging":"Open with the customer's own failure rate converted into lost revenue, not with M1's global-growth line or M4's average uplift."},
  "decider":{"covered":true,"evidence":[
    {"id":"E6","excerpt":"The CFO, Martin. Lucy was the champion, she wanted it, IT was fine with it. Martin said no.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E7","excerpt":"Lucy told me. I never met him.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E8","excerpt":"Lucy said he doesn't take vendor meetings and she'd carry it.","label":"fact"},

   "insight":"The CFO held the decision, and everything we know about him comes through Lucy. Once access to Martin was refused, our only route to him was the material Lucy carried into the room, and we never built that material for a CFO. The controller also shaped the decision by writing the one-pager, and we had no contact with them at all.","messaging":"When the economic buyer won't meet vendors, give the champion a CFO-ready page in finance language that can stand in the room without us."},
  "competitor":{"covered":true,"evidence":[
    {"id":"E9","excerpt":"They were on Fiserv through their bank, had been forever.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E10","excerpt":"when the bank heard, they came back and sharpened the rate.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E11","excerpt":"No new product, nothing. Just a better rate.","label":"opinion"},
    {"id":"E13","excerpt":"After the bank came back, every email was the rate.","label":"fact"}],
   "insight":"The incumbent didn't address declines at all. It cut its rate, and that alone moved the whole conversation from declines to rate. We followed it there instead of pulling it back to the failed orders, so we ended up competing on the bank's terms. Whether the rate cut fixed anything about the declines was apparently never put to the customer.","messaging":"When an incumbent counters on rate, answer with what the cheaper rate still leaves unfixed: the same one-in-twelve failed orders at a lower per-transaction cost."},
  "message":{"covered":true,"evidence":[
    {"id":"E12","excerpt":"Up to then Lucy was asking about declines.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E15","excerpt":"Lucy was nodding the whole way.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E26","excerpt":"We showed the uplift slide. The average improvement in acceptance.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E16","excerpt":"Silence, honestly, nothing bombed. It was a good cycle. We lost on price.","label":"opinion"}],
   "insight":"Farah's explanation of why big-ticket orders get declined landed with the champion. The generic average-uplift slide (M4) did not survive the trip to the CFO, who concluded it was 'the same thing'. The rep's claim that nothing got silence is contradicted by the outcome: the value story drew no response from the decider.","messaging":"Rewrite M4 from an average uplift into the customer's own declines on big baskets, and treat M6 and M8 as support for that figure, not substitutes for it."},
  "decided":{"covered":true,"evidence":[
    {"id":"E18","excerpt":"Right before that she'd been telling me it was a formality.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E17","excerpt":"he's not going to pay more for the same thing.","label":"quote"},
    {"id":"E19","excerpt":"The controller did a one-pager for Martin. Our rate, their rate, side by side.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E22","excerpt":"Our quote.","label":"fact"}],
   "insight":"The deal was lost on a page our team never saw, built by a controller we never met, holding only rate lines and our quote. Martin's line 'the same thing' shows the page carried no difference in outcome. In the rep's own words the comparison also left out the gateway fee and the chargeback headcount, so it wasn't even a full comparison of costs. The champion calling it a formality points to a judgment error on her side and ours.","messaging":"Always provide the decision page ourselves, comparing total cost plus revenue recovered, so the customer never compares rate against rate."},
  "gaps":{"covered":true,"evidence":[
    {"id":"E37","excerpt":"Lucy asked once if we had something she could hand Martin. Like a one-page business case.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E38","excerpt":"I sent her the deck and the pricing proposal.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E29","excerpt":"Farah offered to run their declines. She wanted a three-month export so she could show what the failed orders were worth.","label":"fact"},
    {"id":"E32","excerpt":"...Nothing from us. I assume Lucy told him.","label":"opinion"}],
   "insight":"The missing piece wasn't a product capability but a proof asset. Lucy asked for a one-page business case and got the deck and a price. The analysis that would have filled it, Farah's decline export, was offered and then dropped to protect a quarter-end close. Whether Martin ever heard what the failed orders were costing is unknown.","messaging":"Build a one-page business case template based on a decline export (failed orders, their value, total cost against the incumbent) and make it a standard step before pricing goes to finance."},
  "language":{"covered":true,"evidence":[
    {"id":"E40","excerpt":"orders dying at the last step.","label":"quote"},
    {"id":"E41","excerpt":"the big baskets.","label":"quote"},
    {"id":"E42","excerpt":"we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no.","label":"quote"},
    {"id":"E24","excerpt":"Why would I pay more for the same thing.","label":"quote"}],
   "insight":"The champion talks about lost sales and wasted effort: orders dying, big baskets, the card saying no. We talk about authorization rates and acceptance uplift. The CFO's only recorded words, relayed through Lucy, are 'the same thing', which shows our language never reached him as a difference.","messaging":"Lead with 'orders dying at the last step' and the big-basket greenhouse sale that dies when the card says no, and keep 'authorization rate' as the explanation underneath."}},
 "close":{"gaps":[
   {"question":"Which part of our pitch got silence?","kind":"dodged","follow_up":"Ask Sam and Farah which slides or claims drew no questions from Lucy or IT, especially the uplift slide and customer stories."},
   {"question":"What did Martin have in front of him about what the failed orders were costing?","kind":"unknown","follow_up":"Ask Lucy (via Sam) whether she raised the one-in-twelve failure rate or its revenue impact with Martin, and how he responded."},
   {"question":"Would matching the price have won the deal?","kind":"dodged","follow_up":"Ask Sam to reconcile 'the rate is what killed it' with his own point that Martin would still see 'same rate, so why move'. Ask Lucy whether a matched rate would have changed Martin's answer."},
   {"question":"How serious was the IT lead's concern about moving before spring?","kind":"unknown","follow_up":"Ask Lucy or the IT lead whether a post-spring migration date would have changed anything, and whether that timing is now a reopening window."},
   {"question":"How did our quoted rate compare to the bank's sharpened rate, and what did the full cost comparison look like?","kind":"unknown","follow_up":"Ask Sam whether Lucy can share the controller's one-pager, and whether the gateway fee and chargeback headcount could be quantified for a revisit."}],
  "rep_takeaway":"When a champion asks for 'something she could hand' the decider, treat it as the deal itself, not an errand. The decline export Farah offered was the business case, and skipping it to save two weeks at quarter-end left the CFO comparing two rates and seeing 'the same thing'."},
 "confidence":"medium"}

header.tag_why: The CFO was looking at a one-pager that compared rate lines and nothing else, and we never put a price on what Fernbrook's own failed orders cost, so he read us as charging more for 'the same thing'.

evidence.excerpt: Their ecommerce director, Lucy, came inbound.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: She said about one in twelve online orders was failing at the payment step, and it was worse on the big baskets.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Her number. Off their own dashboard.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: she couldn't get a straight answer from the processor on why.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: The deal began with a measurable revenue leak: one in twelve online orders failing, worse on high-value items, and the figure came from the customer's own dashboard. We had a number we could have priced from the first call. A second pain, the incumbent's lack of explanation, went unused even though Lucy raised it herself.
trigger.messaging: Open with the customer's own failure rate converted into lost revenue, not with M1's global-growth line or M4's average uplift.

evidence.excerpt: The CFO, Martin. Lucy was the champion, she wanted it, IT was fine with it. Martin said no.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Lucy told me. I never met him.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Lucy said he doesn't take vendor meetings and she'd carry it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Martin and the controller. I wasn't in the room. Lucy presented it.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: The CFO held the decision, and everything we know about him comes through Lucy. Once access to Martin was refused, our only route to him was the material Lucy carried into the room, and we never built that material for a CFO. The controller also shaped the decision by writing the one-pager, and we had no contact with them at all.
decider.messaging: When the economic buyer won't meet vendors, give the champion a CFO-ready page in finance language that can stand in the room without us.

evidence.excerpt: They were on Fiserv through their bank, had been forever.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: when the bank heard, they came back and sharpened the rate.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: No new product, nothing. Just a better rate.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: After the bank came back, every email was the rate.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: The incumbent didn't address declines at all. It cut its rate, and that alone moved the whole conversation from declines to rate. We followed it there instead of pulling it back to the failed orders, so we ended up competing on the bank's terms. Whether the rate cut fixed anything about the declines was apparently never put to the customer.
competitor.messaging: When an incumbent counters on rate, answer with what the cheaper rate still leaves unfixed: the same one-in-twelve failed orders at a lower per-transaction cost.

evidence.excerpt: Up to then Lucy was asking about declines.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Lucy was nodding the whole way.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We showed the uplift slide. The average improvement in acceptance.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence, honestly, nothing bombed. It was a good cycle. We lost on price.
evidence.label: opinion

message.insight: Farah's explanation of why big-ticket orders get declined landed with the champion. The generic average-uplift slide (M4) did not survive the trip to the CFO, who concluded it was 'the same thing'. The rep's claim that nothing got silence is contradicted by the outcome: the value story drew no response from the decider.
message.messaging: Rewrite M4 from an average uplift into the customer's own declines on big baskets, and treat M6 and M8 as support for that figure, not substitutes for it.

evidence.excerpt: Right before that she'd been telling me it was a formality.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: he's not going to pay more for the same thing.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: The controller did a one-pager for Martin. Our rate, their rate, side by side.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Our quote.
evidence.label: fact

decided.insight: The deal was lost on a page our team never saw, built by a controller we never met, holding only rate lines and our quote. Martin's line 'the same thing' shows the page carried no difference in outcome. In the rep's own words the comparison also left out the gateway fee and the chargeback headcount, so it wasn't even a full comparison of costs. The champion calling it a formality points to a judgment error on her side and ours.
decided.messaging: Always provide the decision page ourselves, comparing total cost plus revenue recovered, so the customer never compares rate against rate.

evidence.excerpt: Lucy asked once if we had something she could hand Martin. Like a one-page business case.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I sent her the deck and the pricing proposal.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Farah offered to run their declines. She wanted a three-month export so she could show what the failed orders were worth.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: ...Nothing from us. I assume Lucy told him.
evidence.label: opinion

gaps.insight: The missing piece wasn't a product capability but a proof asset. Lucy asked for a one-page business case and got the deck and a price. The analysis that would have filled it, Farah's decline export, was offered and then dropped to protect a quarter-end close. Whether Martin ever heard what the failed orders were costing is unknown.
gaps.messaging: Build a one-page business case template based on a decline export (failed orders, their value, total cost against the incumbent) and make it a standard step before pricing goes to finance.

evidence.excerpt: orders dying at the last step.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: the big baskets.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Why would I pay more for the same thing.
evidence.label: quote

language.insight: The champion talks about lost sales and wasted effort: orders dying, big baskets, the card saying no. We talk about authorization rates and acceptance uplift. The CFO's only recorded words, relayed through Lucy, are 'the same thing', which shows our language never reached him as a difference.
language.messaging: Lead with 'orders dying at the last step' and the big-basket greenhouse sale that dies when the card says no, and keep 'authorization rate' as the explanation underneath.

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam and Farah which slides or claims drew no questions from Lucy or IT, especially the uplift slide and customer stories.

gaps.question: What did Martin have in front of him about what the failed orders were costing?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy (via Sam) whether she raised the one-in-twelve failure rate or its revenue impact with Martin, and how he responded.

gaps.question: Would matching the price have won the deal?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam to reconcile 'the rate is what killed it' with his own point that Martin would still see 'same rate, so why move'. Ask Lucy whether a matched rate would have changed Martin's answer.

gaps.question: How serious was the IT lead's concern about moving before spring?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy or the IT lead whether a post-spring migration date would have changed anything, and whether that timing is now a reopening window.

gaps.question: How did our quoted rate compare to the bank's sharpened rate, and what did the full cost comparison look like?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam whether Lucy can share the controller's one-pager, and whether the gateway fee and chargeback headcount could be quantified for a revisit.

close.rep_takeaway: When a champion asks for 'something she could hand' the decider, treat it as the deal itself, not an errand. The decline export Farah offered was the business case, and skipping it to save two weeks at quarter-end left the CFO comparing two rates and seeing 'the same thing'.
